introFrames: The story of Aquinas is one of faith, opportunity and community, shaped by generations who have made a difference in our communities and the wider world.
Our heritage is deeply woven into the College’s identity, grounded in the Catholic faith, founded by the Christian Brothers in 1894 and shaped by the values of Edmund Rice.
This timeline celebrates the people, places and moments that have shaped Aquinas and carried the spirit of Edmund Rice forward.
acknowledgement: As we celebrate our history, we also acknowledge its painful chapters. Young people in Christian Brothers schools were failed by those who should have protected them. In the 2017 Apology to Victims and Survivors of Sexual Abuse, Edmund Rice Education Australia acknowledged the profound and lasting harm caused, as well as a history of denial, secrecy and barriers to redress. That acknowledgement remains part of an ongoing commitment to truth-telling, healing, safeguarding and ensuring the dignity and wellbeing of every child and young person.

entries.title: An extraordinary life begins in Callan
paragraphs: Edmund Rice was born on his family’s farm at Westcourt, near Callan in County Kilkenny, Ireland. The fourth of seven sons, he grew up alongside his brothers and two stepsisters in a loving and comfortable Catholic home where his parents, Robert and Margaret, guided their family in faith and Gospel spirituality.
These early influences would remain with Edmund throughout his life and ultimately shape an educational mission that would reach far beyond Ireland.

image.alt: Birthplace of Edmund Rice in Callan
image.sourceLabel: Birthplace of Edmund Rice in Callan

entries.title: A young man finds his way
paragraphs: After leaving school, Edmund was apprenticed to his uncle in the busy port town of Waterford. Intelligent, enterprising and a man of integrity, he became a successful and respected businessman.

Edmund’s upbringing and strong faith shaped the way he saw the world around him. Despite his growing prosperity, he remained deeply aware of the poverty and hardship on the streets of Waterford and, together with like-minded friends, became increasingly involved in offering comfort, care and practical support to people in need.

entries.title: A new chapter
paragraphs: Edmund married Mary Elliott, the daughter of a local Catholic family, and the couple began life together with great hope for their future and the children they hoped to raise.

entries.title: Faith through heartbreak
paragraphs: Edmund’s life changed profoundly when Mary died following an accident, leaving him to care for their baby daughter, also called Mary, who had been born with additional needs.

Grieving the loss of his wife, Edmund drew deeply on his faith and devoted himself to his daughter’s care. The experience of love, loss and vulnerability made him even more compassionate to others experiencing hardship.

entries.title: Education changes everything
paragraphs: Edmund could not ignore the poverty he saw around him and felt called to action.

It was at this time that one of Edmund’s friends, Mary Power, helped him to recognise his true mission was to help children in need, and he became convinced that education could offer more than mere knowledge. It could give them faith, dignity, confidence, and the freedom to shape a better future.

With restrictions against Catholic education easing, Edmund opened a school for impoverished boys in a converted stable in Waterford. Demand quickly outgrew the little classroom and in 1803 Edmund used his own wealth to establish a much larger school on an elevated site overlooking the city. Mount Sion included classrooms and accommodation for Edmund and his companions, together with a bakery and tailor that helped provide food, clothing and practical support for students.
It was a liberating and faith-filled education, and the beginnings of a mission that continues today.

entries.title: A mission shared
paragraphs: Edmund was inspired by Nano Nagle, who decades earlier had courageously established schools for poor girls in Cork and founded the Presentation Sisters.
Following her example, Edmund and his companions committed themselves through religious vows to a life of faith, service and education.
What had begun with one extraordinary man responding to the needs he saw around him was becoming a lifelong calling.

entries.title: From Waterford to the world
paragraphs: Schools inspired by Edmund’s vision continued to open across Ireland, giving thousands of boys who might otherwise have been excluded from education the opportunity to learn and flourish.
On 5 September 1820, Pope Pius VII formally approved the Congregation of Christian Brothers.

entries.title: A legacy lives on
paragraphs: Edmund retired as Superior General of the Christian Brothers in 1838 and returned to Waterford for his final years.
Blessed Edmund Ignatius Rice died on Thursday 29 August 1844, surrounded by his companions. He was buried at Mount Sion, where the school he established continues more than two centuries later.
Edmund’s legacy lived on through the communities, schools and people who had embraced his belief in faith, education, dignity and opportunity for all.

entries.title: The mission reaches Australia
paragraphs: Led by Br Patrick Ambrose Treacy, the Christian Brothers arrived in Melbourne, bringing the educational mission begun by Edmund Rice to Australia.
From those beginnings, Christian Brothers’ schools would soon spread across the country, offering liberating education and Gospel spirituality to Australian students.

entries.title: Our Perth story begins
paragraphs: Christian Brothers’ College Perth opened on the corner of St Georges Terrace and Victoria Avenue in the heart of the city.

It marked the beginning of the story that would eventually become Aquinas College, grounded in the same belief that inspired Edmund Rice in Waterford: that education can open new possibilities, and that true strength is found in standing with others through justice and solidarity.

entries.title: The first boarders
paragraphs: Perth was changing rapidly during the gold rush and families were arriving from throughout Australia and beyond.
CBC Perth welcomed its first boarders, giving boys from regional areas access to a Catholic education and establishing a Boarding tradition that would become an enduring part of the Aquinas story.

For generations to come, boys from regional, rural and remote communities would make the College their home during the school term, celebrating an inclusive community and adding to the vibrant culture of Perth’s most respected Catholic boys’ school.

entries.title: Founding the PSA
paragraphs: CBC Perth joined the Church of England Grammar School (now Guildford Grammar School), High School (now Hale School) and Alexander Scotch College (now Scotch College) as the four founding members of the Public Schools’ Association.

The new association created regular interschool sporting competition and began a tradition of rivalry, teamwork, sportsmanship and sporting excellence that remains a distinctive part of Aquinas life today.

entries.title: Looking beyond the city
paragraphs: CBC Perth was growing and space in the centre of Perth was becoming increasingly limited.

Plans emerged to move the Boarding students to a new campus where there would be room to live, learn and play. The Depression delayed those ambitions, but by the mid-1930s attention had turned to a remarkable stretch of land on the Mount Henry Peninsula.
A new chapter was beginning to take shape.

entries.title: Finding a new home
paragraphs: The Christian Brothers purchased 254 acres of elevated land on the Mount Henry Peninsula from the Manning family for £9,925.

With bushland, river frontage and room to grow, the site offered something the city location never could: the opportunity to create a new campus shaped by its natural surroundings, with space to expand and the river at its doorstep.

entries.title: Aquinas takes shape
paragraphs: Archbishop Prendiville laid the foundation stone for Aquinas College on the Mount Henry Peninsula.
Around it, an enormous transformation was underway. Land was cleared for what would become Redmond Oval and work began to establish the facilities needed for the College’s first students.
The following year, a boatshed appeared on the banks of the Canning River, beginning an association between Aquinas and the river that remains central to College life.

entries.title: Welcome to Aquinas
paragraphs: Aquinas College opened at Mount Henry with 160 boarders and 55 day students.
The new College inherited CBC Perth’s colours, honours and membership of the PSA, carrying more than four decades of history with it into its new home.
A boatshed on the banks of the Canning River also allowed rowing to thrive at Mount Henry, continuing a tradition that would connect generations of Aquinians to the river.

entries.title: Making room to play
paragraphs: Creating a College from bushland required considerable physical effort, much of it undertaken by members of the community.
As the playing fields expanded, Lynch Oval to the west and McMahon Oval to the east were named in honour of two teachers whose tireless work helped clear and prepare the land.
The landscape Aquinians know today was quite literally being lovingly shaped by the people who called the College home.

entries.title: Honouring fallen Aquinians
paragraphs: Thanks to the generosity of the College community, the College’s premier sporting field, Memorial Oval, was established and dedicated to Aquinians who had lost their lives in war.

Fundraising for the ground was organised by the Old Aquinians’ Association committee, raising $5,000 and commencing a lasting legacy of philanthropy and community support that continues today with the Aquinas College Foundation.
The Memorial Oval scoreboard was named in recognition of the first Headmaster at Aquinas, Br C. Placidus Foley, and his significant contribution to the College.

entries.title: New spaces for learning
paragraphs: The Murphy Wing became Aquinas’ first purpose-built classroom block.

Named after Br V.I. Murphy, Headmaster from 1951 to 1956, the building contained classrooms, science laboratories, a hall, gymnasium, music centre and library, offering more learning opportunities for students.

The Chaplain’s residence was also built at the southern end of the Main Building. Today it is the Ken Kelsall Heritage Centre, home to the College Archives and named after Aquinas’ first College Captain.

entries.title: A growing College
paragraphs: Western Australia was changing rapidly after the Second World War, and new suburbs brought more families to the area surrounding Aquinas.
Day student numbers grew considerably and a second secondary school stream was introduced, with a third following by 1960.
The expansion also led to a significant increase in lay teachers, beginning a gradual transformation in the staff who would share responsibility for the education and care of Aquinas students.

entries.title: One story, two Colleges
paragraphs: CBC Perth relocated from the city to East Perth and became Trinity College. The shared heritage of CBC Perth would now thrive through two Colleges.
At Mount Henry, Aquinas continued to grow. The Senior Block was completed towards the end of the year and construction began on a new Junior Classroom Block.

entries.title: Junior School opens
paragraphs: The Aquinas Junior School was officially opened by Minister for Education the Hon. E.M.H. Lewis on 7 April.
The College now had 673 enrolled students, including 510 in the Senior School, 163 in the Junior School and 234 boarders.
Within five years, enrolments would reach 817 as Aquinas continued to develop into the College community familiar today.

entries.title: A spiritual home
paragraphs: The Chapel of St Thomas Aquinas officially opened on 12 August, with Bishop Goody celebrating Mass for the College community, who had lovingly planned and worked hard for their new spiritual space.

Over the decades, generations of Aquinians and their families would gather together in the beautiful Chapel for prayer, celebration, reflection, grief, music and many of the significant moments of College life.

entries.title: A new landmark rises
paragraphs: The original Edmund Rice Administration Building was expanded with a five-storey addition designed to complement its original three-storey southern wing.

Overlooking the playing fields and Canning River, it became one of the most recognisable features of the campus and remains a strong visual link between the Aquinas of today and its earlier years at Mount Henry and CBC Perth.

image.alt: Celebrating the extension of the Edmund Rice Administration Building
image.sourceLabel: Celebrating the extension of the Edmund Rice Administration Building

entries.title: A home for hockey
paragraphs: The Mike Kinsella Hockey Pavilion opened beside the College playing fields.
Created through the combined support of the Old Aquinians’ Hockey Club and the College, it provided a home for both alumni and school hockey.

It was also an early example of something that would become increasingly important at Aquinas: facilities created not only for students of the day, but as places where generations could continue to meet and belong.

entries.title: A new home on the river
paragraphs: The Br N.N. Wilson Boatshed opened on the banks of the Canning River, replacing the original 1938 boatshed and giving the College’s flourishing Rowing program a new home.

image.alt: Opening of the Br NN Wilson Boatshed
image.sourceLabel: Opening of the Br NN Wilson Boatshed

entries.title: Learning beyond the classroom
paragraphs: Aquinas became one of the first schools in Western Australia to build a 50-metre swimming pool, with the first Inter-House swimming competition held there at the beginning of the year.

The Redmond Learning Centre was completed and named in honour of Br M.F. Redmond, who served the Aquinas community for more than 45 years. Now known as the Veritas Centre, it reflected an understanding of the different spaces, experiences and approaches through which boys learn.

entries.title: Making and creating
paragraphs: The Manual Arts Centre opened, giving students greater opportunities to create, design, make and express themselves.
It reflected a broadening view of education at Aquinas, recognising that talent and learning can take many forms, from the practical and technical to the imaginative and artistic.

entries.title: A place to come together
paragraphs: With generous support from families and Old Aquinians through the Br Redmond Memorial Building Fund, a new Hall and Gymnasium opened.

Known as the Angelicvm, the building incorporated a stage and drama area and became an important home for assemblies, performances, sport and community events. Today, the space houses the College Library.

Its distinctive façade features a sculptural relief by Perth artist Hans Arkeveld that captures the story of Aquinas on the external view, and a concern with human rights on the wall inside the building’s foyer.

entries.title: A stronger sense of belonging
paragraphs: A vertical House system was introduced within Boarding, establishing Gibney, Nunan, Keaney and Pinder Boor Houses.
By bringing boys of different ages together, the system created smaller communities within Boarding and encouraged friendships, leadership and support across year groups.

entries.title: Boarding transformed
paragraphs: Boarding at Aquinas entered a new era with the opening of four purpose-built Boarding House facilities.

Made possible through the generosity of the College community and the Aquinas 2000 fundraising initiative, the new Houses contained homely spaces designed around central social areas and spacious bedrooms for the comfort of boarders.

Nestled in the Peninsula bushland with easy access to the river, the Boarding village is a space with spirit. Fishing, rowing, bike tracks, playing fields and courts offer plenty of opportunities for boys to be active, explore and enjoy life beyond the classroom.

image.alt: Architect Gerald Bosich, Archbishop Foley and Headmaster Br Carrigg at the Opening of the Boarding Houses
image.sourceLabel: Architect Gerald Bosich, Archbishop Foley and Headmaster Br Carrigg at the Opening of the Boarding Houses

entries.title: Parents and Friends of Aquinas
paragraphs: Aquinas College Parents & Friends Association was established under Aquinas parent, Brian Sierakowski.
It gave parents another way to participate in College life and formalised a culture of volunteering, friendship and practical support that had long been part of Aquinas.

entries.title: One hundred years
paragraphs: Aquinas celebrated the centenary of the founding of Christian Brothers’ College Perth and a century of Catholic education in the Edmund Rice tradition in Western Australia.
The year provided an opportunity to celebrate those who had shaped the College while looking towards the next century.

Building on the success of the Boarding model, the House system was also introduced across the Secondary School, supporting strong pastoral care and creating new opportunities for students of different ages to connect, participate and lead.

entries.title: In the spirit of Edmund Rice
paragraphs: For generations, Aquinas families and Old Aquinians had rallied behind projects that would strengthen the College for those who followed.
The Aquinas College Foundation was established to build on and formalise that extraordinary tradition of giving.
Through bursaries and support for significant College projects, the Foundation has created an enduring way for one generation to help create opportunities for the next.

entries.title: A new era of leadership
paragraphs: Mr Robert White became the first lay Headmaster of Aquinas College, marking a significant moment in the evolution of leadership that had begun with the Christian Brothers more than a century earlier.
Overlooking the Canning River, the Hughes Dining Hall and Waterford Room opened, creating new spaces where boarders could share daily life and the wider College community could come together.

Br Regis Hughes arrived in Perth in 1896 and tirelessly travelled throughout the state to raise funds to assist with the establishment of CBC Perth. The Waterford Room commemorates the city where Edmund Rice began his work in the education and care of boys.

entries.title: New life for a historic space
paragraphs: The Mary Kerr Arts Centre, housed within part of the original 1938 College building, underwent an extensive refurbishment.

The project created generous studios for a new generation of young artists, its soaring ceilings and heritage elements providing an inspirational space while retaining an important piece of Aquinas history.

entries.title: Faith in action
paragraphs: The Mount Sion Religious Formation Centre opened, providing a dedicated home for faith, mission, identity and Christian Service Learning.

The Centre helped connect belief with action, encouraging students to look beyond themselves, encounter people and communities with different experiences, and recognise their capacity to contribute to a more just and compassionate world.

entries.title: Pavilion enhances Oval
paragraphs: The Churack Pavilion opened overlooking Memorial Oval.

Its construction was made possible through the generosity of members of the College community, including Old Aquinian Geoff Churack and his family, and created another place for students, families, Old Aquinians and visitors to come together around College life.

entries.title: The mission continues
paragraphs: With the Christian Brothers ageing and declining in numbers, the responsibility for the governance of Aquinas and other Christian Brothers’ schools across the nation was passed to Edmund Rice Education Australia.

The change marked a new chapter. The mission begun by Edmund Rice and carried by generations of Christian Brothers would now be shared through a broader community of lay and religious leaders, staff, families and students.
The EREA Touchstones would provide a contemporary expression of that mission through Liberating Education, Gospel Spirituality, Inclusive Community, and Justice and Solidarity.

image.alt: Christian Brothers Oceania Province is established
image.sourceLabel: Christian Brothers Oceania Province is established

entries.title: Walking alongside others
paragraphs: Aquinas students embarked on the College’s first overseas immersion to the Philippines as part of the Christian Service Learning program.

The experience invited students to encounter communities very different from their own, listen to their stories and learn through relationship rather than simply viewing service as something done for others.
It began an enduring tradition of immersion, cultural learning and solidarity that challenged Aquinians to consider their place and responsibilities in a wider world.

entries.title: Designing the future
paragraphs: The former Manual Arts facility reopened as the Design and Technology Building, providing contemporary spaces in which students could design, experiment, problem-solve and turn ideas into reality.

Today, the D&T workshops and studios help Aquinians to learn important skills and develop their pathways to the future through a number of learning qualifications that provide direct access to their goals.

entries.title: A school built for boys
paragraphs: The Br Paull Centre opened as a major new sporting and community facility.

The stunning building provides a versatile space for indoor sport, assemblies and other activities. The busy hub for sport, Health and Physical Education and Outdoor Education was named in honour of Br Kevin Paull, the last Christian Brother to serve as Headmaster of Aquinas College, creating an enduring connection between the College’s heritage and a facility designed for future generations of Aquinians.

entries.title: The journey begins earlier
paragraphs: The Early Learning Centre opened and Aquinas welcomed its first Kindergarten students
For the first time, the Aquinas journey could begin in the earliest years of a boy’s education, extending the College from Kindergarten through to Year 12.

entries.title: Canteen upgrade
paragraphs: A new College Canteen opened, providing a contemporary facility for students and staff and expanding the essential service of feeding the community

entries.title: At the heart of Boarding
paragraphs: A new Headmaster’s Residence was completed on the College grounds.
Located close to Boarding, the house enables the Headmaster to be more involved in the daily life of the residential community and the wider campus.

entries.title: A new home for younger boarders
paragraphs: The new Brothers House opened, creating a welcoming home for the College’s younger Boarding students and restoring a four-House structure to the community.

The Year 7 Quadrangle was also developed, creating a dedicated space in which boys beginning Secondary School could establish friendships, build confidence and find their place within the wider College.

entries.title: Mary and Jesus
paragraphs: A sculpture of Mary and Jesus by artist Nathan Stewart was unveiled in the Year 7 Quadrangle.

Placed within the everyday life of the campus, the work offered students a quiet reminder of faith, love and the relationship between a mother and her son who is preparing to step out on his own path.

image.alt: Statue of Mary and Jesus by Nathan Stewart
image.sourceLabel: Statue of Mary and Jesus by Nathan Stewart

entries.title: Renewing a spiritual heart
paragraphs: The Chapel of St Thomas Aquinas underwent a major refurbishment, increasing its capacity and adding a mezzanine while carefully retaining the character of a place cherished by generations of Aquinians.
The same year saw the establishment of the Aquinas College Schola Cantorum, giving boys the opportunity to experience the rich tradition of sacred choral music.
Through its demanding rehearsal and performance program, the Schola brought together faith, music, discipline and community, enriching liturgies and celebrations at Aquinas and beyond.

entries.title: A new stage for Aquinas
paragraphs: The Aquinas Centre will open near the entrance to the College, creating a new home for the performing arts and a place where the wider community can come together.
At its heart will be the Recital Hall, alongside rehearsal, teaching, performance and recording spaces designed to give boys opportunities to create, collaborate and perform.

More than a new building, the Aquinas Centre represents another step in a story that began with a small classroom in Waterford: creating places where young people can discover what they are capable of and share those gifts with others.
